chapter_note.about: Counting is how you answer 'how many ways?' without listing every way. This chapter rebuilds six tools: the multiplication and addition principles, factorials, permutations, combinations, arrangements with repeats or blocks, and counting by complement. Everything grows from one move: split the job into stages and multiply the choices. These tools feed discrete maths and every probability chapter, where a probability is often favourable ways divided by total ways.
chapter_note.simple: Counting means working out how many possibilities there are without writing them all down. If you make one choice and then another, you multiply the number of options, like picking a shirt and then trousers. Lining up friends uses the same idea with fewer options each time, and that gives a factorial. When the order does not matter, such as picking a team, you count the line-ups and divide out the repeats. Sometimes it is easier to count what you do not want and subtract it from everything. These few moves answer most counting questions.

concept_map.title: Factorials: lining up n items
concept_map.one_line: n different things in a row: n!. Cancel, do not multiply out.

concept_map.title: Permutations: ordered picks
concept_map.one_line: Pick r of n with order: n(n-1)... with r factors.

concept_map.title: Combinations: unordered picks
concept_map.one_line: Divide the ordered count by r! when only the group matters.

concept_map.title: Arrangements with repeats and blocks
concept_map.one_line: Divide n! by each repeat factorial; glue "together" items.

concept_map.title: Counting by complement, and 2^n
concept_map.one_line: At least one = total minus none; n in-or-out choices give 2^n.

cards.title: Multiplication and addition principles
cards.simple: Think of ordering a combo at a canteen: you pick one starter and then one main. With 2 starters and 3 mains, each starter can go with every main, so you get 2 groups of 3 meals. That is 2 × 3 = 6, not 2 + 3. You only add when you pick from separate lists and take just one thing, such as one drink that is either tea or coffee. 'And then' means multiply. 'Or' means add. In exam words: the multiplication principle (rule of product) multiplies the options of independent stages, and the addition principle (rule of sum) adds the options of cases that cannot happen together.
cards.idea: To count the ways to do a job in stages, **multiply** the number of choices at each stage. If the first stage has 2 options and the second stage has 3 options for every first choice, there are $2\times3=6$ outcomes. If you instead pick **one thing from one of two separate lists**, you **add** the list sizes.
cards.definition:
$$\text{stages: }n_1\times n_2\times\cdots\times n_k\qquad\text{either-or lists: }m+n$$

$n_i$ is the number of choices at stage $i$. $m$ and $n$ are the sizes of two lists with nothing in common, and you pick from only one of them. Words that signal multiply: 'and then', 'followed by', 'each'. Words that signal add: 'or', 'either'.
cards.intuition_full: Draw the choices as a tree. The first stage splits the start into branches, one per option. Every branch then splits again, one branch for each option of stage two. Each path from the start to a tip is one complete outcome, so the number of outcomes is the number of tips. When every branch splits into the same number of children, tips = branches × children, which is why the stages multiply. For either-or there is no second split: the lists sit side by side and you count both, so you add. A good check is to fix the first choice and ask how many ways are left. If that number is the same whatever the first choice was, multiply. Only the count has to be the same at each stage, not the options themselves.

examples.setup: A café set meal is one starter followed by one main. There are 2 starters (Soup, Salad) and 3 mains (Rice, Pasta, Wrap). How many different set meals are there?
steps: Stage 1, the starter, has 2 choices: Soup or Salad.
Pick Soup. Stage 2 still offers 3 mains, so Soup leads to 3 meals.
Pick Salad. The same 3 mains are available, so Salad also leads to 3 meals.
Count the tips of the tree: each tip is one full meal, and $3+3=6$.
The same answer in one line: 2 groups of 3 is $2\times3=6$.

examples.setup: From city P to city Q there are 3 roads, and from Q to city R there are 4 roads. There are also 2 direct roads from P to R. How many different routes go from P to R?
steps: A route via Q is a road P to Q **and then** a road Q to R.
Routes via Q: $3\times4=12$.
Direct routes: 2. A route is either via Q **or** direct, never both.
examples.answer: 14 routes. Multiply inside a route, add across the two kinds of route.

examples.setup: How many 3-digit numbers are even? Digits may repeat, and the first digit cannot be 0.
steps: Three slots: hundreds, tens, ones. The rules sit on the first and last slots.
Hundreds: any of 1 to 9, so 9 choices (0 is not allowed).
Tens: any digit 0 to 9, so 10 choices.
Ones: must be even (0, 2, 4, 6, 8), so 5 choices.
Multiply: $9\times10\times5=450$.
examples.answer: 450. Each slot has its own count, rules included, and the counts multiply.

cards.why: Almost every counting question, from passwords to seating plans, is the multiplication principle in disguise. Without it you would list outcomes one by one. In GATE: counting strings, functions, relations and codes in discrete maths, and the size of a sample space in probability.
how: Split the job into stages, in the order you would do it.
Draw one slot per stage and write the number of choices in each: _ × _ × _.
Fill the restricted slots first (first digit not 0, last digit even).
Multiply the slot counts. If the job splits into separate cases, work out each case and add.
cards.mistake: Adding where you should multiply, or the reverse. 2 starters and 3 mains give 6 meals, not 5. Ask whether the choices happen one after the other (multiply) or you pick from one list **or** another (add).
edge_cases: A stage with 0 choices makes the whole product 0: with no mains available there are 0 meals.
Repeats allowed keeps every slot the same size ($10^3$ three-digit strings). Repeats banned shrinks later slots ($10\times9\times8$).
A slot with a rule (not 0, must be even) is counted first, or later counts depend on what you did.
Cases that overlap cannot simply be added: the either-or rule needs lists with nothing in common.
connections: Used in: Discrete maths. Counting strings, functions ($|B|^{|A|}$) and relations all start here.
Used in: Probability. The size of a sample space for repeated trials is a product (3 coin tosses: $2^3=8$).

cards.title: Factorials: lining up n items
cards.simple: You have 4 friends and 4 chairs in a row. Anyone can sit in the first chair, so 4 choices. Whoever is left can take the second chair, so 3 choices, then 2, and the last friend has just 1. Multiplying 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 gives 24 different seatings. That chain of multiplying down to 1 has its own name and symbol: 4!. In exam words: n! (n factorial) is the number of ways to arrange n different objects in a row, and 0! is defined as 1.
cards.idea: To arrange $n$ different things in a row, any of the $n$ can go first, then $n-1$ are left for the second place, and so on down to 1. The total is $n\times(n-1)\times\cdots\times1$, written **$n!$**. Four friends in four chairs give $4!=24$ seatings.
cards.definition:
$$n!=n\times(n-1)\times(n-2)\times\cdots\times2\times1,\qquad 0!=1$$

$n$ is a whole number. Useful identity: $n!=n\times(n-1)!$, so $\dfrac{n!}{(n-2)!}=n(n-1)$. Values to know: $3!=6$, $4!=24$, $5!=120$, $6!=720$, $7!=5040$.
cards.intuition_full: Factorials grow very fast because each extra item multiplies the total by the new size: 4 items give 24, 5 give 120, 6 give 720. The key habit is cancelling. Because $n!=n\times(n-1)!$, a ratio such as $\frac{9!}{7!}$ collapses: write $9!=9\times8\times7!$ and cancel $7!$ to get $72$. You never need to multiply out big factorials. The value $0!=1$ is not a trick: there is exactly one way to arrange nothing (do nothing), and the rule $n!=n\times(n-1)!$ only works at $n=1$ if $0!=1$. Another way to see $n!$: put the first item down, then each new item can be slipped into a growing number of gaps, 2 gaps, then 3, then 4, and so on, and these gap counts multiply to $n!$.

examples.setup: 4 friends A, B, C, D sit in 4 chairs in a row. In how many different ways can they sit?
steps: Fill the chairs from left to right. Chair 1 can take any of the 4 friends: 4 choices.
Say B sits in chair 1. Chair 2 can take any of the 3 friends who are left.
Say D takes chair 2. Chair 3 has 2 friends left to choose from.
Say A takes chair 3. Chair 4 gets the 1 friend left, C: no real choice.
Multiply the choices: $4\times3\times2\times1=24=4!$.
Expand the top until it reaches $(n-1)!$: $(n+1)!=(n+1)\times n\times(n-1)!$.
Cancel $(n-1)!$ from the top and the bottom. The ratio is $(n+1)\times n$.
Solve $n(n+1)=90$: two consecutive numbers with product 90 are $9\times10$.

examples.setup: Five people stand in a queue and Rhea must be at the front. How many queues are possible? Then: what is $0!$ and why?
steps: Rhea is fixed in position 1: that slot has 1 choice.
The other 4 people fill the other 4 positions in any order: $4!=24$.
Total: $1\times24=24$.
$0!$: arranging 0 people leaves exactly one arrangement (the empty queue), so $0!=1$.

cards.why: Factorials count line-ups, and they sit inside permutations and combinations. Reading and cancelling them quickly saves marks. In GATE: simplifying expressions like $\frac{n!}{(n-2)!}$ and counting orderings inside permutation and probability questions.
how: Name the slots (positions) and count how many items can fill each, left to right.
If all $n$ different items are used once each, the answer is $n!$.
With one item fixed in place, remove it and arrange the rest: $(n-1)!$.
To simplify a ratio, expand the bigger factorial until it matches the smaller one, then cancel.
cards.mistake: Multiplying out a big factorial before cancelling, or treating $n!$ as $n\times n$. $5!=120$, not $25$. Cancel first: $\frac{8!}{6!}=8\times7$. Also, $(n-1)!$ is **not** $n!-1$.
edge_cases: Factorials need whole numbers: $2.5!$ is not defined at this level.
If some items are identical, $n!$ over-counts. See the repeats card.
connections: Used in: Discrete maths. Permutations $\frac{n!}{(n-r)!}$, combinations and the binomial theorem are all built from factorials.
Used in: Probability. Random orderings and shuffles use $n!$ as the total number of outcomes.
Used in: Algorithms. A brute-force search over all orderings costs $n!$ steps, which grows faster than $2^n$.

cards.title: Permutations: ordered picks
cards.simple: A club of 7 people needs a President, a Secretary and a Treasurer, all different. The President can be any of the 7. The Secretary has to be someone else, so 6 choices. The Treasurer: 5 choices. That makes 7 × 6 × 5 = 210. You stopped after 3 picks instead of using up all 7 people. A shortcut is to take 7! and cancel the part you did not use, which is 4!. In exam words: a permutation is an ordered selection of r items from n, and ⁿPᵣ = n!/(n−r)!.
cards.idea: A **permutation** picks $r$ items from $n$ different items **where order matters**, for example who gets which job. The first pick has $n$ options, the next has $n-1$, and so on for $r$ picks. Choosing a President, Secretary and Treasurer from 7 people gives $7\times6\times5=210$.
cards.definition:
$${}^nP_r=n(n-1)(n-2)\cdots(n-r+1)=\frac{n!}{(n-r)!}$$

$n$ is how many items you pick from and $r$ is how many positions you fill. The product has exactly $r$ factors. The factorial form works because dividing by $(n-r)!$ cancels the unused tail of $n!$.
cards.intuition_full: Each of the $r$ positions is a slot, and filling slots in order is the multiplication principle with shrinking choices, because an item that is already used cannot be used again. Write $n!$ as $n\times(n-1)\times\cdots\times1$. A permutation uses only the first $r$ factors and ignores the rest, which is the tail $(n-r)!$. Dividing by the tail removes it: $\frac{7!}{4!}=7\times6\times5$. If $r=n$ you use every factor and get $n!$, so a full line-up is the special case. Order matters when swapping two chosen items gives a different outcome: President Asha with Secretary Bilal is a different result from President Bilal with Secretary Asha.

examples.setup: A club has 7 members. In how many ways can a President, a Secretary and a Treasurer be chosen (three different people)?
steps: Three posts are filled in order, and nobody can hold two posts.
President: any of the 7 members.
Secretary: any of the 6 members left.
Treasurer: any of the 5 members left.
Multiply the three counts: $7\times6\times5=210$.
As a factorial: $7!$ has seven factors, but the posts use only the first three.
The unused tail $4!$ cancels: $\frac{7!}{4!}=7\times6\times5=210$.

examples.setup: A lock code has 4 different digits chosen from 0 to 9 (a code may start with 0). How many codes are possible?
steps: Four slots, digits cannot repeat, order matters: it is $^{10}P_4$.
Slot 1: 10 digits. Slot 2: 9. Slot 3: 8. Slot 4: 7.
$10\times9\times8\times7=5040$.
Check with the formula: $\frac{10!}{6!}=10\times9\times8\times7=5040$.

examples.setup: Evaluate $^4P_4$, $^4P_1$ and $^4P_0$, and say what $^3P_5$ should be.
steps: $^4P_4=\frac{4!}{0!}=24$: picking all 4 is just the factorial.
$^4P_1=\frac{4!}{3!}=4$: one slot, four choices.
$^4P_0=\frac{4!}{4!}=1$: filling no slots has exactly one way (do nothing).
$^3P_5$: five slots but only 3 people, so you run out. There are 0 ways.

cards.why: Permutations are the counting tool for rankings, codes and anything where position matters. In GATE: seating and ranking questions, digit and password counts without repeats, and the numerator of many probability fractions.
how: Ask: if I swap two chosen items, is the outcome different? If yes, order matters.
Count the slots $r$ and the pool $n$.
Write $n\times(n-1)\times\cdots$ with exactly $r$ factors.
Use $\frac{n!}{(n-r)!}$ only to simplify, never to multiply out big factorials.
cards.mistake: Using all of $n!$ when only $r$ positions are filled. Choosing 3 officers from 7 is $7\times6\times5=210$, not $7!=5040$. Count the factors: there should be exactly $r$ of them.
edge_cases: If $r>n$ there are 0 permutations.
With repeats allowed it is $n^r$ instead, since every slot keeps all $n$ choices.
connections: Used in: Discrete maths. The number of one-to-one functions from an $r$-element set into an $n$-element set is $^nP_r$.
Used in: Probability. 'All different' outcomes, such as no two people sharing a birthday, are permutation counts.
Used in: Combinations. Divide $^nP_r$ by $r!$ to forget the order; that is the next card.

cards.title: Combinations: unordered picks
cards.simple: Now pick 2 people from 4 friends for a pair, where the pair has no order: Asha and Bilal is the same pair as Bilal and Asha. If you count 'first pick, second pick' you get 4 × 3 = 12 line-ups. But each pair got counted twice, once as AB and once as BA. So the real number of pairs is 12 ÷ 2 = 6. In general, count the ordered picks, then divide by the number of ways to shuffle the chosen group. In exam words: a combination ⁿCᵣ counts the r-element subsets of an n-element set, and ⁿCᵣ = ⁿPᵣ / r!.
cards.idea: A **combination** picks $r$ items from $n$ when only **who is chosen** matters, not the order. Count the ordered picks first, then divide by the $r!$ orders in which the same group could have been picked. Choosing 2 of 4 people: $\frac{4\times3}{2}=6$ pairs.
cards.definition:
$$\binom nr={}^nC_r=\frac{n!}{r!\,(n-r)!}=\frac{{}^nP_r}{r!}$$

$n$ is the pool size and $r$ is the group size. Read $\binom nr$ as 'n choose r'. It satisfies $\binom nr=\binom n{n-r}$, $\binom n0=\binom nn=1$ and $\binom n1=n$.
cards.intuition_full: Think of the 12 ordered pairs as a table where each real pair shows up twice: AB and BA, AC and CA, and so on. Grouping the mirror images shrinks 12 to 6. For bigger groups, each chosen set of $r$ people can be lined up in $r!$ ways, so the ordered count is exactly $r!$ times the combination count. That gives $\binom nr=\frac{^nP_r}{r!}$. The symmetry $\binom nr=\binom n{n-r}$ has a one-line reason: choosing the $r$ people who join is the same as choosing the $n-r$ who stay out. It also gives a shortcut, because $\binom{11}9$ is easier as $\binom{11}2$. When a job needs several separate selections, such as 2 defenders and 3 attackers, work out each $\binom nr$ and multiply them.

examples.setup: From 4 people A, B, C, D, how many different pairs can be chosen? The order inside a pair does not matter.
steps: List the ordered picks (first, second): $4\times3=12$ of them.
Regroup them so that mirror images sit together: AB with BA, AC with CA, and so on.
AB and BA name the same two people, so they count as one pair.
Every pair appears exactly twice, so keep one per column: $12\div2=6$ pairs.
In symbols: $\binom42=\frac{^4P_2}{2!}=\frac{12}{2}=6$.

examples.setup: A team needs 2 defenders chosen from 7 players and 3 attackers chosen from 4 players. How many teams are possible?
steps: Two separate selections, each unordered. Defenders: $\binom72=\frac{7\times6}{2}=21$.
Attackers: $\binom43=\binom41=4$ (choosing the 3 who play is choosing the 1 who rests).
The two selections are independent stages, so multiply: $21\times4=84$.
examples.answer: 84 teams. Choose each group with nCr, then join the groups with the multiplication principle.

examples.setup: Evaluate $\binom{11}{9}$ without a long calculation, and say how many ways there are to choose 0 people from 6.
steps: $\binom{11}9=\binom{11}{11-9}=\binom{11}2$: choosing the 9 who join is the same as choosing the 2 who stay out.
$\binom60=1$: there is exactly one way to choose nobody, the empty group.

cards.why: Most 'select', 'choose' or 'form a committee' questions are combinations, and many probabilities are a ratio of two of them. In GATE: committee and team selection, counting subsets of a given size, and drawing-without-replacement probabilities.
how: Ask: if I swap two chosen items, is the outcome the same? If yes, order does not matter.
Compute $\binom nr$ as $\frac{n(n-1)\cdots}{r!}$ with $r$ factors on top.
Use symmetry when $r$ is large: replace $r$ with $n-r$.
For several selections done together, compute each $\binom nr$ and multiply.
cards.mistake: Using $^nP_r$ when order does not matter, which over-counts by a factor of $r!$. Another slip is adding two selections instead of multiplying them: choosing 2 defenders **and** 3 attackers gives $21\times4$, not $21+4$.
edge_cases: $\binom nr=0$ when $r>n$.
$\binom n0=\binom nn=1$.
$\binom nr=\binom n{n-r}$.
$\binom{n}{r}+\binom{n}{r+1}=\binom{n+1}{r+1}$ (Pascal's rule), the rule behind Pascal's triangle.
connections: Used in: Probability. The binomial distribution has $\binom nk$ in front, and 'draw 2 cards from 52' uses $\binom{52}2$.
Used in: Discrete maths. The number of subsets of size $r$ of an $n$-set is $\binom nr$, and handshakes or possible edges among $n$ nodes number $\binom n2$.
Used in: Algebra. The numbers $\binom nr$ are the coefficients in $(a+b)^n$.

example.setup: From 4 people A, B, C, D, how many different pairs can be chosen? The order inside a pair does not matter.
steps: List the ordered picks (first, second): $4\times3=12$ of them.
Regroup them so that mirror images sit together: AB with BA, AC with CA, and so on.
AB and BA name the same two people, so they count as one pair.
Every pair appears exactly twice, so keep one per column: $12\div2=6$ pairs.
In symbols: $\binom42=\frac{^4P_2}{2!}=\frac{12}{2}=6$.

cards.what: A **combination** picks $r$ items from $n$ when only **who is chosen** matters, not the order. Count the ordered picks first, then divide by the $r!$ orders in which the same group could have been picked. Choosing 2 of 4 people: $\frac{4\times3}{2}=6$ pairs.
cards.what_full:
A **combination** picks $r$ items from $n$ when only **who is chosen** matters, not the order. Count the ordered picks first, then divide by the $r!$ orders in which the same group could have been picked. Choosing 2 of 4 people: $\frac{4\times3}{2}=6$ pairs.

$$\binom nr={}^nC_r=\frac{n!}{r!\,(n-r)!}=\frac{{}^nP_r}{r!}$$

$n$ is the pool size and $r$ is the group size. Read $\binom nr$ as 'n choose r'. It satisfies $\binom nr=\binom n{n-r}$, $\binom n0=\binom nn=1$ and $\binom n1=n$.

**Worked example.** From 4 people A, B, C, D, how many different pairs can be chosen? The order inside a pair does not matter.

1. List the ordered picks (first, second): $4\times3=12$ of them.
2. Regroup them so that mirror images sit together: AB with BA, AC with CA, and so on.
3. AB and BA name the same two people, so they count as one pair.
4. Every pair appears exactly twice, so keep one per column: $12\div2=6$ pairs.
5. In symbols: $\binom42=\frac{^4P_2}{2!}=\frac{12}{2}=6$.

**Answer:** 6 pairs.
cards.why_full:
Most 'select', 'choose' or 'form a committee' questions are combinations, and many probabilities are a ratio of two of them. In GATE: committee and team selection, counting subsets of a given size, and drawing-without-replacement probabilities.

Foundation, used in: dm.counting, prob.counting, prob.discrete.
cards.trap: Using $^nP_r$ when order does not matter, which over-counts by a factor of $r!$. Another slip is adding two selections instead of multiplying them: choosing 2 defenders **and** 3 attackers gives $21\times4$, not $21+4$.

cards.title: Arrangements with repeats and blocks
cards.simple: Take the letters A, A, B. If the two A's were different (say one red and one blue), you could line the three up in 3 × 2 × 1 = 6 ways. But the A's look the same, so swapping them changes nothing. Each real word got counted twice, so there are only 6 ÷ 2 = 3 different words: AAB, ABA, BAA. For 'sit together' problems, glue the two people into one block, arrange the blocks, then remember the pair can flip inside the block. In exam words: with repeated items the count is n! divided by the factorial of each repeat count, and for 'together' you treat the group as one object and multiply by its internal arrangements.
cards.idea: If some of the $n$ items are **identical**, count as if all were different, then divide by the ways to shuffle each identical group, because those shuffles change nothing. If some items must stay **together**, glue them into one block, arrange the blocks, then arrange inside the block.
cards.definition:
$$\frac{n!}{n_1!\,n_2!\cdots n_k!}$$

$n$ is the total number of items, and $n_1,n_2,\dots$ are the sizes of the groups of identical items (an item that appears once contributes $1!=1$). For a block of $m$ items that must stay together among $n$ items in total, the count is $(n-m+1)!\times m!$.
cards.intuition_full: Label the identical items to tell them apart: A₁ and A₂. Now all items are different and there are $n!$ arrangements. Rub the labels off: arrangements that differ only by swapping A₁ and A₂ turn into the same word. Every real word appears exactly $2!$ times among the labelled ones, because that is how many ways the two A's can be swapped. So divide by $2!$. With three identical items you divide by $3!=6$. For blocks, think of two friends holding hands: while they hold hands they move as one unit, so you arrange fewer units. But the pair can stand either way round, so multiply by the internal order. 'Not together' is then easiest by complement: all arrangements minus the 'together' ones, which is the idea of the last card.

examples.setup: Find the number of different arrangements of the letters in AAB.
steps: Pretend the A's differ: A₁, A₂, B. There are $3!=6$ orders.
Pair them up: A₁A₂B with A₂A₁B, A₁BA₂ with A₂BA₁, BA₁A₂ with BA₂A₁. Each pair differs only by swapping the A's.
Rub off the labels: each pair becomes one word (AAB, ABA, BAA).
Each word was counted $2!=2$ times, so keep one of each: 3 words.
In symbols: $\frac{3!}{2!}=3$.

examples.setup: How many distinct arrangements of the letters of PEPPER are there?
steps: 6 letters: P three times, E twice, R once.
If all were different: $6!=720$.
Divide by the shuffles of each repeated letter: $3!$ for P, $2!$ for E, $1!$ for R.

examples.setup: Five people stand in a row. Two of them, Dev and Esha, must stand next to each other. How many ways? Then: how many ways have them not next to each other?
steps: Glue Dev and Esha into one block. Now there are 4 units: the block and 3 others.
Arrange the 4 units: $4!=24$.
Inside the block, Dev and Esha can swap: $2!=2$.
Together: $24\times2=48$.
All arrangements: $5!=120$. Not together = all minus together $=120-48=72$.

cards.why: Words with repeated letters and 'together' seating plans are standard 2-mark counting questions, and the same division by repeats sits inside combinations. In GATE: arranging the letters of a word, seating with conditions, and counting binary strings with a fixed number of 1s.
how: Count the items and list the repeat counts.
Start from $n!$ as if everything were different.
Divide by $k!$ for each group of $k$ identical items.
For 'together', make a block, arrange the units, then multiply by the block's internal orders.
For 'not together', use all minus together.
cards.mistake: Forgetting the internal order of a block (answering 24 instead of 48 above), or dividing by the repeat count itself instead of its factorial. For three identical letters divide by $3!=6$, not by 3.
edge_cases: If all items are different, the formula is just $n!$.
Two separate blocks of sizes $m_1$ and $m_2$: arrange all the units, then multiply by $m_1!\times m_2!$ for the orders inside.
A binary string of length $n$ with $k$ ones has $\frac{n!}{k!\,(n-k)!}=\binom nk$ arrangements: repeats and combinations are the same count.
A fixed position (first letter must be P) is handled by removing that letter and arranging the rest.
connections: Used in: Discrete maths. Counting words, strings and multisets uses this division.
Used in: Probability. Equally likely orderings of coloured balls use $\frac{n!}{a!\,b!}$.
Used in: Combinations. $\frac{n!}{k!\,(n-k)!}$ is the same formula, so $\binom nk$ counts strings with $k$ ones.

check.q: How many different arrangements do the letters of BOOK have?
In how many ways can 3 red and 2 blue identical balls be put in a row?
Three people stand in a row and two of them must be together. How many ways?
check.a: Block the two: $2!$ units arranged, times $2!$ inside, $=2\times2=4$.

cards.title: Counting by complement, and 2^n
cards.simple: Suppose you toss a coin three times and want the outcomes with at least one head. Listing them is annoying. It is quicker to count all the outcomes, which is 8, and throw away the one outcome with no head at all (TTT). That leaves 7. This works because 'at least one' is the opposite of 'none', and 'none' is usually a single easy case. A similar trick counts the subsets of a set: each element is either in or out, 2 choices each, so n elements give 2 × 2 × ... = 2ⁿ subsets. In exam words: complement counting means total minus unwanted, and a set with n elements has 2ⁿ subsets.
cards.idea: When a condition like 'at least one' is awkward to count directly, count **everything** and subtract the cases that break the condition. A choice between two options repeated $n$ times (in or out, heads or tails, 0 or 1) gives $2^n$ outcomes, so a set with $n$ elements has $2^n$ subsets.
cards.definition:
$$\text{wanted}=\text{total}-\text{unwanted}\qquad\text{number of subsets of an }n\text{-set}=2^n$$

'Total' is the count with no condition. 'Unwanted' is the count of outcomes that fail the condition (for 'at least one' that means 'none'). The number of subsets of size $r$ is $\binom nr$, and all sizes together add up to $2^n$.
cards.intuition_full: 'At least one' means one or more, and the direct count splits into many cases (exactly one, exactly two, and so on). The opposite case, 'none', is a single case. Counting the opposite and subtracting turns a long job into a short one. For binary strings of length $n$, each position has two choices, so there are $2^n$ strings. The string with no 1 is just 00...0, so 'at least one 1' has $2^n-1$ strings. Subsets and strings are the same thing: write 1 under each element you include and 0 under each you leave out. That is why a set with $n$ elements has $2^n$ subsets, from the empty set (all 0s) to the full set (all 1s). A proper subset leaves out the full set, so a set has $2^n-1$ proper subsets.

examples.setup: How many 3-bit strings (like 010) contain at least one 1?
steps: Each of the 3 bits has 2 choices, so there are $2\times2\times2=8$ strings in all.
Direct counting is awkward (one 1, or two 1s, or three 1s), so count the opposite.
The opposite of 'at least one 1' is 'no 1 at all': only 000.
Subtract: $8-1=7$.
Check by listing: the other seven strings, 001 to 111, each have a 1.

examples.setup: A set has 5 elements, $S=\{1,2,3,4,5\}$. How many subsets contain at least one even number?
steps: Total subsets: each element is in or out, so $2^5=32$.
The opposite of 'at least one even' is 'no even number': the subset uses only the odd elements 1, 3, 5.
Subsets of $\{1,3,5\}$: $2^3=8$ (the empty set included).

examples.setup: A fair die is rolled 3 times. In how many of the outcomes does at least one 6 appear?
steps: Total outcomes: $6\times6\times6=216$.
No 6 on any roll: each roll has 5 choices, $5\times5\times5=125$.
At least one 6: $216-125=91$.
Direct counting would need three cases: exactly one 6 ($75$), exactly two ($15$) and exactly three ($1$), which also add to $91$.
examples.answer: 91 outcomes. The complement works for any number of options, not just two.

cards.why: 'At least one' appears constantly in counting and probability, and the complement turns a long case split into one subtraction. The count $2^n$ covers subsets, binary strings and truth-table rows. In GATE: 'at least one' selections, number of subsets or relations, and the probability of 'at least one success'.
how: Spot the words 'at least', 'not all' or 'not together'.
Count the total with no condition.
Count the opposite case (none, all, or together).
Subtract: wanted = total minus opposite.
For in-or-out choices over $n$ items, write $2^n$.
cards.mistake: Subtracting the wrong opposite. The opposite of 'at least one head' is 'no heads', not 'exactly one head'. Another slip is forgetting the empty set: $2^n$ includes it.
edge_cases: The empty set and the full set are both subsets, so a set has $2^n-1$ non-empty subsets.
A proper subset excludes the full set too, so there are $2^n-1$ proper subsets.
'At most' can also flip: at most 2 of 5 = total minus (exactly 3, 4 or 5) when that is shorter.
The total and the unwanted counts must follow the same rules, or the subtraction is meaningless.
connections: Used in: Discrete maths. The power set has $2^n$ elements, a relation on $n$ elements is a subset of $n\times n$ pairs so there are $2^{n^2}$ of them, and a truth table with $n$ inputs has $2^n$ rows.
Used in: Probability. $P(\text{at least one})=1-P(\text{none})$ is the same trick.
Used in: Digital logic. $n$ bits give $2^n$ different values.

check.q: How many 4-bit strings are there? And how many contain at least one 1?
check.a: $2^4=16$ strings, and $16-1=15$ have at least one 1.

check.q: How many subsets does a 3-element set have?
Two dice are rolled. In how many of the 36 outcomes does at least one die show a 6?

scenes.title: Set meals as a tree: 2 starters times 3 mains

steps.caption: Stage 1, the starter: 2 choices, Soup or Salad. Each choice starts its own branch.
Pick Soup. Stage 2 still offers 3 mains (R = Rice, P = Pasta, W = Wrap), so Soup leads to 3 meals.
Pick Salad. The same 3 mains are available, so Salad also leads to 3 meals.
Count the tips of the tree. Each tip is one complete meal: 3 + 3 = 6.
Two groups of three is the same as multiplying the choices: $2\times3=6$.
Fill the chairs from left to right. Chair 1 can take any of the 4 friends: 4 choices.
Say B sits in chair 1. Chair 2 can take any of the 3 friends who are left.
D takes chair 2. Chair 3 has 2 friends left to choose from.
A takes chair 3. Chair 4 has only 1 friend left, so there is no real choice.
C takes the last chair. Multiply the choices: $4\times3\times2\times1=24$, written $4!$.

scenes.title: Three posts from seven members, in order

steps.caption: Three posts are filled in order, from 7 members, and nobody can hold two posts.
President: any of the 7 members.
Secretary: any of the 6 members left.
Treasurer: any of the 5 members left.
Multiply the three counts: $7\times6\times5=210$ ways.
As a factorial: $7!$ has seven factors, but the three posts use only the first three.
The unused tail $4\times3\times2\times1=4!$ cancels. So $^7P_3=\frac{7!}{4!}=210$.

scenes.title: Choosing 2 of 4: ordered picks, then pairs

steps.caption: Ordered picks: a first person and then a second person. That gives $4\times3=12$ lists.
Regroup the list so that mirror images share a column: AB with BA, AC with CA, and so on.
AB and BA name the same two people, so together they count as one pair. Every column works this way.
Keep one entry per column. Every pair was listed twice, so the 12 lists shrink to 6 pairs.
In symbols: divide the ordered count by $2!$, the number of orders of a pair. $\binom42=6$.
Pretend the two A's differ: A₁, A₂, B. There are $3!=6$ orders. Each column holds two orders that differ only by swapping the A's.
Swap the two A's and A₁A₂B becomes A₂A₁B. Once the labels are rubbed off, both read AAB.
Rub off all the labels. Each column now shows the same word twice.
Keep one word per column: AAB, ABA, BAA. Each was counted $2!=2$ times.
In symbols: $\frac{3!}{2!}=3$. Divide $n!$ by the factorial of each repeat count.

scenes.title: Three-bit strings with at least one 1

steps.caption: Each of the 3 bits is 0 or 1, so there are $2\times2\times2=8$ strings in all.
"At least one 1" splits into cases: one 1, two 1s, three 1s. Count the opposite instead.
The opposite is "no 1 at all". Only one string qualifies: 000.
Wanted = total minus unwanted: $8-1=7$.
Check: the other seven strings, 001 to 111, each contain a 1.
